title: Thomas More
hook: the king's good servant, but God's first, executed for refusing the oath

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cranmer's hand, held in the fire before the rest of him. Your line was this hand first. What did you own, plainly, before anyone had to ask? Day eight hundred seventy.

There's a portrait of him, painted in his lifetime. A dark coat trimmed with fur. A heavy gold chain across his shoulders, the mark of a man in the king's service. A face that looks clever and a little tired. Lawyer. Writer of a book called Utopia. Friend of the king, and for a time Lord Chancellor of England. Under the fine coat, tradition says, he wore a rough shirt of hair against his skin, to keep himself humble. Then the king broke with Rome, and asked for an oath. And the man in the gold chain went quiet. Today: Thomas More.
screen: `A GOLD CHAIN AND A FUR COAT.`

segments.voice: More stepped down as chancellor as Henry pulled the church in England away from Rome. Then came the oath. Leading men of the realm were asked to swear to Henry's new marriage and the new order behind it. More, as the usual account goes, was willing to accept who would inherit the crown, but he would not swear to words that set aside the pope's authority over the church. He refused, and he also refused to say why. He hoped silence would protect him, since he had said nothing against the king. He was sent to the Tower of London. His daughter Margaret visited him there and begged him to give way. He didn't. In the end he was tried, convicted on testimony he said was false, and beheaded. Tradition reports that on the scaffold he said he died the king's good servant, but God's first. Notice the order of those words. He doesn't call himself the king's enemy. He calls himself the king's servant, and a good one. He just won't put the king first. Peter and the apostles, ordered by the council in Jerusalem to stop preaching, said it in the King James Bible: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Catholics honor More as a saint and a martyr of conscience. There is more to remember. As chancellor, More pursued Protestants hard. He wrote fierce books against William Tyndale, and some of the people he hunted as heretics were burned. The story holds both pieces of the man. Brave and hard, holy and fierce. A conscience that would not bend for a king, and a chancellor who pressed hard on the consciences of others.
screen: `HE REFUSES THE OATH, AND STAYS SILENT.`
`THE KING'S GOOD SERVANT, BUT GOD'S FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your first loyalty clear. Settle, and breathe. Name, quietly, the things that ask for your loyalty: work, family, friends, a team, a country, a cause, a faith. Don't rank them yet. Just let them line up. Then ask: if two of these ever pulled against each other, which one would I keep? Don't argue with the answer. Just hear it. If you pray, you can bring that question to God and stay with it. If you don't, just let it settle in you. The bell holds the time.
Thomas More. Lawyer, writer and chancellor of England, executed for refusing Henry's oath, remembered as saying he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
Your line: god's first. Today, when two loyalties pull at you, notice which one you reach for first, and whether you'd choose it again. Day eight hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Thomas More as a saint and martyr, keeping his feast together with John Fisher's, and he is honored as a patron of statesmen and politicians; Anglicans and others also remember him for his conscience.

fork.setup: you're Thomas More, in the Tower. your daughter begs you to swear the oath and come home. what do you do?
options: refuse, and keep silent about why.
fork.reveal: he refuses, and stays silent. he is tried anyway, and tradition reports he died the king's good servant, but God's first.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint who stood up to a king.
what it means: a man who called himself the king's good servant, and would not put the king above God.
what a scholar hears: the same conscience that would not bend had pressed hard against Protestants as chancellor, so the story keeps both pieces.

notes: Editor pass: cut the superlative 'one of the highest offices in the land' and 'famous' portrait; changed 'Christians hold both pieces' (a sweeping claim) and the closing 'few could imagine' judgment to a plain two-sided line about More.
Claims rule: no dates. 'the king's good servant, but God's first' is given as 'tradition reports', paraphrased without quotation marks (from a contemporary newsletter account). Confirm.
The terms of the oath: More reportedly would accept the succession but not the oath as framed (rejecting papal authority); attributed to 'the usual account'. Confirm.
'Convicted on testimony he said was false' (Richard Rich's testimony); confirm phrasing.
Hair shirt given as 'tradition says' (Roper); Holbein portrait described without naming the painter. 'one of the highest offices in the land' is general; confirm or trim.

Honest balance: More's pursuit of Protestants as chancellor and his books against Tyndale; 'some of the people he hunted as heretics were burned'. A Catholic Keeper should confirm the tone is fair, and a Protestant reader that it is not softened.
Last line 'in an age when few could imagine letting others' consciences go free' is a general historical judgment; trim if a Keeper prefers.
howItsDone: shared feast with John Fisher (Catholic calendar, 22 June) and patronage of statesmen and politicians; Anglican commemoration claim is general; confirm.
Second editor pass: 'honest tellings' (used twice, implying other tellings are dishonest) replaced with plain lines; howItsDone patronage changed to statesmen and politicians.
Audit pass: the Holbein portrait predates his chancellorship, and the chain is a collar of royal service, not the chancellor's chain of office; hook reworded.
